item.title: EEG Resting-State Beta Band Dynamic Functional Connectivity Reveals State-Dependent Disruption of Language Network Lateralisation in First-Episode Schizophrenia.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Language disorganisation is a core feature of schizophrenia with significant functional consequences. However, its neurophysiological substrates remain poorly characterised, particularly in the early stages of the illness. This study investigated whether first-episode schizophrenia (FES) is associated with disruption in the organisation of language-network lateralisation, using both static and dynamic functional connectivity metrics in the EEG beta band. Thirty-one FES patients and 32 age-matched healthy volunteer subjects (HVS) underwent resting-state 64-channel EEG. Source-level connectivity was estimated using the weighted phase lag index with sliding windows, yielding 979 connectivity matrices per participant. Brain network states (BNS) were identified via k-means clustering. Static connectivity was obtained by time-averaging. Temporal features, graph-theoretical metrics, and language-network laterality indices were extracted for both whole-network and language-specific analyses. Group comparisons used permutation-based tests with family-wise error correction. Static connectivity yielded no significant group differences in any metric. Dynamic analysis identified six BNS. FES showed a significant increase in the variability of the temporal dynamics and graph-theory features of BNS5, a state characterised by parieto-occipital dominance. The core language network laterality index was significantly reduced in FES within BNS1, a state characterised by auditory-visual dominance. BNS1 occurrence correlated negatively with language disorganisation scores. Dynamic BNS-specific language network metrics correlated with verbal fluency performance exclusively in FES. These findings demonstrate that language dysfunction in early psychosis is expressed as state-dependent disruption of brain network stability and language lateralisation, detectable only through dynamic connectivity analysis.

item.title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human.

item.title: Functional neural activity and connectivity deficits underlying vocal auditory feedback control in post-stroke aphasia: An fMRI study.
item.description:
Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology
Objective This study investigated the functional neural activity and connectivity correlates of disrupted sensorimotor integration underlying vocal production and motor control deficits in post-stroke aphasia. Methods fMRI data were acquired from 15 aphasia and 15 control participants during vocalization of speech vowel sounds under altered auditory feedback with randomized ± 100-cents pitch-shift stimuli. Results We found that stroke-induced brain damage in aphasia was associated with diminished activation within left-hemisphere dorsal stream networks, including premotor and motor cortices, posterior superior temporal regions, and supramarginal gyrus. Functional connectivity analysis revealed reduced left-hemisphere coupling between posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) and dorsal and ventral precentral speech areas (dPSA and vPSA) in aphasia, indicating disrupted auditory-motor integration. Aphasia participants exhibited reduced following and opposing (i.e., compensatory) vocal responses to pitch-shifted auditory feedback, reflecting impairments in both rapid feedforward and slower feedback-based control mechanisms. In addition, impaired vocal compensatory behavior was associated with reduced functional connectivity between pSTG and the left dorsal precentral speech areas (dPSA) as well as the right dorsal laryngeal motor cortex (dLMC), suggesting the critical role of these networks in auditory-feedback-based laryngeal motor control during vocal production and their stroke-induced impairment in aphasia. Conclusions Our data provide converging evidence of disrupted auditory-motor integration and impaired neural communications within dorsal stream networks in aphasia. Significance These findings emphasize that clinical interventions for aphasia therapy benefit from targeting sensorimotor mechanisms supporting vocal auditory feedback processing and control. Personalized interventions that strengthen sensorimotor integration pathways could further enhance recovery of fluent verbal communication.

item.title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388–800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group × task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229–334 ms and 377–538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618–723 ms interval, and a group × task interaction in the 562–636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508–629 ms and 660–800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

item.title: Overt and Covert Speech-State Classification from Tripolar Concentric Ring Electrode EEG: A 4 mm and 10 mm Configuration Study.
item.description:
Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)
Electroencephalography (EEG) speech-state classification is a noninvasive method to identify the brain's overt and covert behavior. The EEG achieved through the scalp is contaminated by artifacts and volume conduction and suffers from poor spatial resolution. We present the first application of small 4 mm tripolar concentric ring electrodes (TCREs) to record the overt and covert EEG signals. In addition, EEG signals were recorded for overt and covert behavior using a 10 mm TCRE as a reference. Data were recorded from 16 participants (4 mm, n=8; 10 mm, n=8). Each participant completed 200 picture-naming trials (100 overt and 100 covert). The analysis includes task-to-baseline root mean square ratios, power spectral density, time frequency representation analysis and participant-wise overt and covert classification using linear discriminant analysis, support vector machines, and EEGNet. The overt speech produced higher task-to-baseline ratios than covert speech. In addition, EEGNet achieved the highest mean accuracy (84.06±15.57%), followed by SVM (81.56±14.23%) and LDA (76.56±15.30%).
